label: HMRC policy paper · 29 October 2026
title: Capital allowances: 50% first-year allowance from January 2027, main rate writing-down allowance cut to 12%
summary: The main rate first-year allowance rises from 40% to 50% for spending from 1 January 2027, while the main rate writing-down allowance falls from 14% to 12% from April 2027. What it means for sole traders and companies buying equipment.
body:
On 29 October 2026 HMRC published a policy paper on two changes to capital allowances announced at Budget 2026. Together they change how quickly businesses get tax relief on equipment such as machinery, tools and other plant.

The two changes

  • The main rate first-year allowance (FYA) increases from 40% to 50%. The increased rate is available for expenditure incurred from 1 January 2027.
  • The main rate writing-down allowance (WDA) falls from 14% to 12% a year, for chargeable periods beginning on or after 1 April 2027 for Corporation Tax and 6 April 2027 for Income Tax.
  • The special rate WDA remains at 6%.

Where an accounting period straddles the change date, a hybrid WDA rate applies, based on the proportion of the period before and after the change.

Who this is aimed at

HMRC explains that full expensing and the £1 million annual investment allowance (AIA) already give full upfront relief for most new plant and machinery. The 40% FYA was introduced at Budget 2025 and has fewer restrictions than full expensing. The stated aim of raising it to 50% is to give more upfront relief to unincorporated businesses and to businesses investing in plant and machinery for leasing.

HMRC also notes that, for many businesses, main rate WDAs are not relevant to future spending, because the AIA or full expensing covers it. The WDA cut mainly affects the balance of spending already sitting in your main rate pool, and any spending not covered by the AIA, full expensing or the FYA.

Who is affected

The policy paper says the changes affect around 600,000 incorporated and unincorporated businesses that claim main rate WDA and main rate FYA. HMRC expects only one-off costs, such as getting familiar with the change and updating software, and no ongoing costs. In rare cases employees who claim WDAs on plant their employer does not provide or reimburse are also affected.

What it means in practice

  • If you are a sole trader or partnership and your spending is within the £1 million AIA, HMRC's paper says the AIA and full expensing already give full upfront relief for most new plant and machinery. These changes matter most where spending goes above that, or for items the AIA does not cover.
  • If your business has a large balance in its main rate pool, the annual WDA on that balance will fall from 14% to 12% for periods starting from April 2027. Relief is not lost, but it is spread over a longer period.
  • The new 50% FYA applies to spending from 1 January 2027, so the timing of a large purchase around that date may affect the relief available in the first year.

What I would do now

  • Check your main rate pool balance in your last accounts or tax computation, so you know how much relief is still to come.
  • If you plan significant equipment purchases, talk to us about which allowance applies (AIA, full expensing or the FYA) and about timing.
  • If your year end straddles April 2027, expect a hybrid WDA rate in that year's computation.

The changes are to be legislated in the Finance Bill. If you would like us to look at your capital allowances position before your next year end, get in touch.
